content: Paul Dudley White was born on June 6, 1886, in Roxbury, Massachusetts, to Herbert Warren White and Elizabeth Abigail Dudley. His early exposure to medicine came from accompanying his father, a family practitioner, on rounds and house calls using a horse and buggy. He graduated from the Roxbury Latin School in 1903 and pursued undergraduate studies at Harvard College, where he studied history, forestry, and pre-medical courses. He earned his M.D. in 1911 and began an internship in pediatrics and internal medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital, where he co-authored his first scientific paper on blood coagulation with Dr. Roger I. Lee. This work led to the development of the Lee-White coagulation time, a method still used to measure blood clotting speed. In 1913, White received a Harvard traveling fellowship to study cardiovascular physiology under Dr. Thomas Lewis in London. This experience, along with the deaths of his sister from rheumatic heart disease and his father from coronary artery disease, profoundly influenced his medical career. During World War I, he served as a medical officer with the British Expeditionary Force in 1916 and the American Expeditionary Force from 1917 to 1919. After the war, he returned to Massachusetts General Hospital as a resident in 1919 and became Chief of the Medical Out-Patient Department in 1920. He joined the Harvard faculty in 1921 as a clinical instructor and rose through the ranks to become an assistant professor in 1933, a clinical professor in 1946, and an emeritus professor in 1949. White resigned as Chief of the Cardiac Service at Massachusetts General Hospital in 1948 to focus on developing the National Heart Institute, following the passage of the National Heart Act signed by President Truman. He was a highly regarded teacher and compassionate physician, publishing 12 books and over 700 scientific articles. His textbook, Heart Disease, first published in 1931, became a classic in the field. His interest in cardiac electrophysiology led to his collaboration with Drs. Louis Wolff and John Parkinson, resulting in the description of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, a condition characterized by rapid heartbeats. On June 28, 1924, White married Ina Helen Reid, a social worker he met while lecturing at the Smith College Training School for Social Work. The couple later adopted two children. White is widely regarded as the founder of preventive cardiology. He served as President Dwight D. Eisenhower's physician after the president's heart attack in 1955 and was a pioneer in promoting the use of the electrocardiogram, as well as advocating for exercise, diet, and weight control to prevent heart disease. In 1924, White co-founded the American Heart Association and served as its president in 1941. He played a key role in establishing the International Association of Cardiology and the International Cardiology Foundation. In 1949, he was named executive director of the National Advisory Heart Council and served as chief consultant to the National Heart Institute from 1948 to 1955. He was instrumental in initiating the Framingham Heart Study, the first major epidemiological study to identify risk factors for coronary artery disease. White also contributed to the American Red Cross and the establishment of the National Institutes of Health. White received numerous international honors and helped establish cardiology organizations worldwide, including in the People's Republic of China, where he was one of the first American physicians to visit. He also collaborated with Soviet physiologist Alexander Filippovich Samoilov, sharing a mutual interest in cardiac electrophysiology. White was a strong advocate for the idea that lifestyle choices influence coronary artery disease. He was among the first to recognize that coronary artery disease could occur in young men and wrote extensively on the subject. He practiced what he preached, maintaining an active lifestyle as a vigorous walker and cyclist. On one occasion, he walked from Washington National Airport to the White House to consult with President Eisenhower. His positive approach reportedly inspired Lyndon B. Johnson to return to the Senate after his heart attack in 1955 and later to become Vice President. In his later years, White continued to travel and lecture on heart disease and increasingly on his concerns for world peace. He passed away in Boston on October 31, 1973, following a second stroke. He was scheduled to receive the Herrick Award from the American Heart Association but died before the honor could be bestowed. A memorial service was held at the Harvard Memorial Church, where a former student delivered a eulogy titled I'm Not Through Yet. In 1986, the United States Postal Service honored White with a 3-cent postage stamp, which remains available today. The 17-mile bike path around the Charles River in Boston is named in his honor.
